\begin{center}
{\Large\textbf{Bayesian mixed models in R: math and syntax for brms and rstanarm}}\\
NRES 746
\end{center}

Both packages fit models by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan and accept
`lme4`-style formulas. Unlike `lmer()` or `glmmTMB()`, they keep the
random effects in the model as parameters and sample them along with
everything else, so a Poisson or binomial model is no harder to fit
than a Normal one. The code pairs below were run on simulated data;
they agree with each other, and with the maximum likelihood fits in the
companion handout (*Mixed models in R: nlme, lme4, and glmmTMB*), up to
Monte Carlo error and the pull of the priors. Each model is written
first in math, then in R.

## Notation

- $i$ indexes observations; $j$ a group (site, stand); $k$ a subgroup
  nested in $j$ (plot within site); $m$ a second, crossed grouping
  (observer); $t$ time. $j[i]$ is the group that observation $i$
  belongs to.
- $\beta$s are fixed effects. Random effects ($a_j$, $b_j$, $v_{jk}$,
  $w_m$) are Normal with mean 0. $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)$ is
  the residual. In a Bayesian model every one of the
  $\beta$s, $\sigma$s, and correlations also gets a prior (section 3).
- The fixed part is written the same way in both packages and in
  `lme4`; so is the random part, for the structures `rstanarm` can fit.

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
\textbf{In the model} & \textbf{Math} & \textbf{brms term (rstanarm, if different)} \\
\midrule
random intercept & $+\,a_{j[i]}$, \ $a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$ & \texttt{(1 | site)} \\
correlated intercept and slope & $(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0}, G)$ & \texttt{(x | site)} \\
uncorrelated intercept and slope & same, with $\rho_{ab} = 0$ & \texttt{(x || site)} \\
nested groups & $+\,a_j + v_{jk}$ & \texttt{(1 | site/plot)} \\
crossed groups & $+\,a_{j[i]} + w_{m[i]}$ & \texttt{(1 | site) + (1 | obs)} \\
AR(1) errors in time & $\eta_t = \phi\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ & \texttt{ar(time = year, gr = plot)} \ (none) \\
residual SD by group & $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{trt}[i]})$ & \texttt{bf(y \textasciitilde{} x, sigma \textasciitilde{} trt)} \ (none) \\
binomial successes & $s_i \sim \text{Binom}(n_i, p_i)$ & \texttt{s | trials(n) \textasciitilde{} x} \ (\texttt{cbind(s, n - s)}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

## 1. Which package when

- **`rstanarm`** (`stan_lmer()`, `stan_glmer()`, `stan_glmer.nb()`)
  ships precompiled Stan programs, so a model starts sampling at once.
  It fits the `lme4` menu (Normal, binomial, Poisson, negative binomial,
  Gamma) with weakly informative default priors that are scaled to the
  data. A good first Bayesian fit when the model is one `glmer()` could
  write.
- **`brms`** (`brm()`) writes a Stan program for each model and compiles
  it (a minute or so the first time). In return it fits nearly anything:
  dozens of families (Student-$t$, beta, zero-inflated and hurdle
  counts, ordinal), residual correlation (`ar()`, Gaussian processes
  `gp()`, spatial `car()`), a model for $\sigma$ or any other
  distributional parameter, nonlinear formulas, and missing-data
  imputation. `stancode(fit)` prints the program, a good starting point
  for writing your own.
- **Stan directly** (`cmdstanr`): latent states, custom likelihoods,
  anything neither formula interface can write.

```
                        rstanarm                       brms
Compile step            none (precompiled)             yes, about 1 min per model
Responses               lme4 families + neg. binomial  many (beta, Student-t, zero-inflated, ...)
Residual correlation    no                             ar(), arma(), gp(), car(), sar()
Unequal variances       no                             bf(y ~ x, sigma ~ trt)
Zero inflation          no                             zero_inflated_*() families, zi ~
Default priors          weakly informative, scaled     flat on slopes; Student-t on intercept, SDs
Covariance prior        decov()                        lkj() on correlations, separate SD priors
Prior-only fit          prior_PD = TRUE                sample_prior = "only"
```

## 2. Random-effect structures

`d` is the data frame; `site`, `plot`, and `obs` (observer) are factors
and `x` is numeric. In every model below, `brm()` and `stan_lmer()` take
the same formula, and `stan_lmer()` can be swapped for `stan_glmer()`
with `family = gaussian`.

**Random intercept.** Observation $i$ in site $j$:
$$y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$$

```{r syntax-ri}
brm(y ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)
```

**Correlated random intercept and slope.**
$$y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + a_j) + (\beta_1 + b_j)\,x_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} a_j \\ b_j \end{pmatrix} \sim
\text{MVN}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\
G = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_a^2 & \rho_{ab}\sigma_a\sigma_b \\
\rho_{ab}\sigma_a\sigma_b & \sigma_b^2 \end{pmatrix}\right)$$

```{r syntax-rs}
brm(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d)
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d)
```

**Uncorrelated random intercept and slope** ($\rho_{ab} = 0$).

```{r syntax-uncorrelated}
brm(y ~ x + (x || site), data = d)
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (x || site), data = d)
```

**Nested groups.** Plot $k$ within site $j$:
$y_{ijk} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ijk} + a_j + v_{jk} + \varepsilon_{ijk}$,
with $v_{jk} \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)$. `site/plot` expands to
`(1 | site) + (1 | site:plot)`.

```{r syntax-nested}
brm(y ~ x + (1 | site/plot), data = d)
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site/plot), data = d)
```

**Crossed groups.** Every observer visits several sites:
$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + a_{j[i]} + w_{m[i]} + \varepsilon_i$,
with $w_m \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)$.

```{r syntax-crossed}
brm(y ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs), data = d)
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs), data = d)
```

`brms` adds two pieces of syntax. `(1 | p | site)` in two formulas of a
multivariate or distributional model correlates the site effects across
them (any label works in place of `p`); `(1 | gr(site, by = trt))`
estimates a separate $\sigma_a$ for each treatment.

## 3. Priors

The correlated random slope model with a prior on every parameter:
$$\beta_0 \sim N(0, 1), \quad \beta_1 \sim N(0, 1), \quad
\sigma_a, \sigma_b \sim \text{half-}N(0, 0.5), \quad
\rho_{ab} \sim \text{LKJ}(2), \quad \sigma_e \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$$
LKJ($\eta$) is a prior on a correlation matrix; for a $2 \times 2$
matrix its density is proportional to $(1 - \rho_{ab}^2)^{\eta - 1}$,
uniform when $\eta = 1$ and pulled toward 0 when $\eta > 1$.

**`brms`** takes one `prior()` per class of parameter, combined with
`c()`, in any order. Classes: `Intercept`, `b` (slopes), `sd`
(random-effect SDs), `cor` (their correlations), and `sigma`. `brms`
bounds SDs at 0, so `normal(0, 0.5)` on `sd` is a half-Normal. The
`coef` and `group` arguments narrow a prior to one parameter, and a
narrower prior overrides a class-wide one.

```{r priors-brms}
get_prior(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d)       # every parameter that can take a prior, with defaults
pri <- c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept),
         prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
         prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = sd),
         prior(normal(0, 0.2), class = sd, group = site, coef = x),   # sigma_b only
         prior(lkj(2), class = cor),
         prior(exponential(1), class = sigma))
brm(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d, prior = pri)
```

**`rstanarm`** has one argument per kind of parameter: `prior` (the
slopes), `prior_intercept`, `prior_aux` ($\sigma_e$, or the negative
binomial's dispersion), and `prior_covariance` (everything in $G$).

```{r priors-rstanarm}
stan_lmer(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d,
          prior_intercept = normal(0, 1), prior = normal(0, 1),
          prior_aux = exponential(1),
          prior_covariance = decov(regularization = 2))
```

`rstanarm` has no separate prior for each SD. `decov()` splits $G$
into a correlation matrix, with an LKJ(`regularization`) prior, and its
variances. The variances add up to $K\tau^2$ for a $K \times K$ matrix,
with a Gamma(`shape`, `scale`) prior on $\tau$, and are divided among
the terms by a Dirichlet(`concentration`) prior. For Normal models the
random-effect SDs are also multiplied by $\sigma_e$, so the default
prior is on their size *relative to* the residual SD.

- **Intercepts.** Both packages put the `Intercept` prior on the
  intercept with every predictor at its *mean*, not at zero.
- **Defaults.** Leave out a prior and each package supplies one:
  `rstanarm` uses Normal priors scaled to the data (`autoscale = TRUE`);
  `brms` uses flat (improper) priors on `b` and Student-$t$ priors
  scaled to the response on the intercept and SDs. `prior_summary(fit)`
  lists what a fit used. Write your own for anything you report.
- **Prior predictive check.** Fit with the priors alone and simulate
  data, to see whether they allow sensible values: `sample_prior =
  "only"` in `brm()`, `prior_PD = TRUE` in `rstanarm`, then
  `pp_check(fit)`.

## 4. Residual correlation and unequal variances (brms only)

`rstanarm` can't fit these; `brms` adds them as terms in the formula.

**AR(1) errors in time.** Plot $j$ in year $t$:
$$y_{jt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{jt} + \eta_{jt}, \qquad
\eta_{jt} = \phi\,\eta_{j,t-1} + \varepsilon_{jt}, \qquad
\varepsilon_{jt} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)$$
`ar[1]` in the output is $\phi$, and `sigma` is the innovation SD
$\sigma_e$ (not the total SD that `gls()` reports).

```{r syntax-ar1}
brm(y ~ x + ar(time = year, gr = plot, p = 1), data = d)               # plots labeled uniquely
brm(y ~ x + ar(time = year, gr = plot, p = 1, cov = TRUE), data = d)   # same model, full covariance
```

The default (`cov = FALSE`) regresses each residual on the previous
one, which is fast but available only for Normal-like families;
`cov = TRUE` builds the AR(1) covariance matrix and works with any
family (adding latent residuals for Poisson or binomial data). `p = 2`
gives AR(2), and `arma(p = 1, q = 1)` an ARMA model.

**Random site intercept plus AR(1) within each plot.**
$y_{jkt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{jkt} + a_j + \eta_{jkt}$, with
$\eta_{jkt}$ AR(1) within plot $jk$.

```{r syntax-ri-ar1}
brm(y ~ x + (1 | site) + ar(time = year, gr = plot), data = d)
```

**Gaps in time.** `ar()` treats the observed times as consecutive, so a
missing year counts as a lag of 1. Add a row for each missing year with
`y = NA`; `mi()` then treats those values as parameters and samples
them, and the AR(1) runs over the full sequence. (Predictors in those
rows must still be filled in.)

```{r syntax-gaps}
brm(bf(y | mi() ~ x + ar(time = year, gr = plot)), data = d_full)
```

**Exponential spatial correlation.** Location $i$ at coordinates
$s_i$, with a smooth spatial surface $f$ plus independent noise:
$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + f(s_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\text{Cov}(f(s_i), f(s_k)) = \alpha^2 e^{-d_{ik}/\ell}$$
`sdgp` is $\alpha$, `lscale` is $\ell$, and `sigma` is the nugget
$\sigma_e$. The maximum likelihood version is
`gls(y ~ x, correlation = corExp(form = ~ east + north, nugget = TRUE))`.

```{r syntax-spatial}
brm(y ~ x + gp(east, north, cov = "exponential", scale = FALSE), data = d)
brm(y ~ x + gp(east, north, k = 20, c = 5/4), data = d)   # approximate GP: much faster for large n
```

`scale = FALSE` keeps $\ell$ in the units of the coordinates. An exact
GP is slow (minutes for 150 locations) and often samples poorly;
expect divergence warnings and a wide posterior for $\ell$, and give
`lscale` an informative prior. The approximate version (`k` basis
functions per dimension) supports only the `exp_quad` and Matérn
kernels. For areal data (counties, watersheds) use `car(M, gr = unit)`
with an adjacency matrix `M`.

**A separate residual SD for each treatment.**
$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\text{trt}[i]}\right)$$
`bf()` takes a formula for $\sigma$ as well as the mean, on the log
scale. With `0 +`, each treatment gets its own $\log\sigma$
(`b_sigma_trta`, ...); exponentiate the draws to get SDs. Any
predictor works (`sigma ~ x` for a variance that changes with $x$), and
so do random effects.

```{r syntax-sigma}
brm(bf(y ~ x, sigma ~ 0 + trt), data = d)
```

Other options: `arma()`, `ma()`, `sar()` (simultaneous autoregressive),
`unstr()` (unstructured within-group correlation), and `fcor()` (a
fixed, known correlation matrix). See `?autocor-terms`.

## 5. Non-Normal responses (GLMMs)

The random effects sit on the link scale, as in `glmer()`.

**Poisson counts.**
$$y_{ij} \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_{ij}), \qquad
\log \lambda_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j$$

```{r syntax-poisson}
brm(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = poisson(), data = d)
stan_glmer(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = poisson, data = d)
```

**Successes $s$ out of $n$ trials.**
$$s_{ij} \sim \text{Binom}(n_{ij}, p_{ij}), \qquad
\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j$$

```{r syntax-binomial}
brm(s | trials(n) ~ x + (1 | site), family = binomial(), data = d)
stan_glmer(cbind(s, n - s) ~ x + (1 | site), family = binomial, data = d)
```

For 0/1 data, `y ~ x + (1 | site)` with `family = bernoulli()` in
`brms`, `family = binomial` in `rstanarm`.

**Overdispersed counts.** Three common choices:

- Negative binomial: $\text{Var}(y_{ij}) = \mu_{ij} + \mu_{ij}^2/\theta$
  with $\log\mu_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j$. $\theta$ is
  `shape` in `brms` and `reciprocal_dispersion` in `rstanarm`
  (`glmmTMB`'s `sigma()`).
- Observation-level random effect: add $o_i \sim N(0, \sigma_o^2)$ to
  the Poisson's $\log\lambda$, one per observation (`obs_id` has a
  unique level for each row).
- Zero-inflated negative binomial (`brms` only): $y_{ij} = 0$ with
  probability $\pi$, otherwise negative binomial as above. `zi ~ 1` is a
  constant $\pi$ on the logit scale; `zi ~ x` lets it vary.

```{r syntax-overdispersed}
brm(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = negbinomial(), data = d)
stan_glmer.nb(count ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)    # or stan_glmer(..., family = neg_binomial_2)
brm(count ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs_id), family = poisson(), data = d)
stan_glmer(count ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs_id), family = poisson, data = d)
brm(bf(count ~ x + (1 | site), zi ~ 1), family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(), data = d)
# brms also: hurdle_negbinomial(), zero_inflated_poisson(), Beta(), student(), Gamma(), ...
```

**Offsets for effort or area.**
$\log\lambda_i = \log A_i + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + a_{j[i]}$; add
`+ offset(log(area))` to the formula in either package.

## 6. Fitting options

```{r fitting}
brm(..., chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 1, backend = "cmdstanr",
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12),
    file = "fits/m1")                  # saves the fit; reruns load it instead of refitting
stan_lmer(..., chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 1, adapt_delta = 0.95)
update(fit, newdata = d2)               # brms: reuses the compiled program when only the data change
```

- `iter` counts warmup, which is half by default; the draws kept are
  `chains * iter / 2`.
- **Check the sampler before the estimates.** $\hat R$ (`Rhat`) near 1
  (above 1.01 is a warning sign), effective sample sizes (`Bulk_ESS`,
  `Tail_ESS` in `brms`; `n_eff` in `rstanarm`) in the hundreds or more,
  and no divergent transitions. Both packages print warnings when these
  fail; `mcmc_plot(fit, type = "trace")` (`brms`) and
  `plot(fit, "trace")` (`rstanarm`) show the chains.
- **Divergent transitions** mean the sampler couldn't follow the
  posterior's shape, so the draws may be biased. Raise `adapt_delta`
  (0.95, then 0.99), tighten priors on the SDs, or simplify the
  random-effect structure. Both packages already use the non-centered
  form for random effects.
- **Model comparison:** `loo_compare(loo(fit1), loo(fit2))` in either
  package gives the elpd difference and its SE. In `brms`,
  `fit <- add_criterion(fit, "loo")` stores the LOO result with the fit.
  Pareto-$k$ warnings mean a few observations dominate the estimate;
  `loo(fit, k_threshold = 0.7)` (`rstanarm`) or `loo(fit, reloo =
  TRUE)` (`brms`) refits the model without each of them.

## 7. Getting results out

```
                      brms                                    rstanarm
Fixed effects         fixef(fit)                              fixef(fit)
Group deviations      ranef(fit)                              ranef(fit)
Group coefficients    coef(fit)                               coef(fit)
Variance components   VarCorr(fit)                            VarCorr(fit)
Summaries, intervals  summary(fit), posterior_summary(fit)    summary(fit), posterior_interval(fit)
All draws             as_draws_df(fit)                        as.data.frame(fit)
Mean predictions      posterior_epred(fit, re_formula = NA)   posterior_epred(fit, re.form = NA)
New observations      posterior_predict(fit)                  posterior_predict(fit)
Posterior pred. check pp_check(fit)                           pp_check(fit)
Effect plots          conditional_effects(fit)                --
Priors used           prior_summary(fit)                      prior_summary(fit)
Stan program          stancode(fit)                           --
```

In the math: `fixef()` gives the $\beta$s, `ranef()` the $a_j$ and
$b_j$, `coef()` each group's $\beta_0 + a_j$ and $\beta_1 + b_j$, and
`VarCorr()` the $\sigma$s and $\rho_{ab}$. In `brms` these return the
posterior mean, SD, and 95% interval; in `rstanarm`, `fixef()`,
`ranef()`, and `coef()` return posterior medians only, so use
`posterior_interval()` or the draws for uncertainty.

- **Anything derived** (a ratio, a peak, a difference between groups) is
  computed draw by draw from `as_draws_df()` or `as.data.frame()`, then
  summarized, so its interval comes for free.
- `posterior_epred()` gives draws of the mean ($\mu$ or $\lambda$);
  `posterior_predict()` adds the observation noise. With
  `re_formula = NA` (`re.form = NA` in `rstanarm`) the random effects
  are set to 0; the default includes them.
- `pp_check(fit)` overlays data simulated from the posterior on the real
  data; `pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "sd")` compares one
  statistic.

## 8. Things that trip people up

- **`re_formula` vs. `re.form`.** `brms` uses `re_formula = NA` (and
  accepts `re.form`); `rstanarm` and `lme4` use `re.form = NA`.
  `rstanarm` silently ignores `re_formula`, so the predictions keep the
  random effects.
- **Variances vs. SDs in the draws.** `rstanarm`'s draws hold the
  entries of $G$ (`Sigma[site:(Intercept),(Intercept)]` is
  $\sigma_a^2$); `brms`'s hold SDs and correlations (`sd_site__Intercept`
  is $\sigma_a$, `cor_site__Intercept__x` is $\rho_{ab}$). `VarCorr()`
  reports SDs in both.
- **Parameter names in `brms`.** `b_x` is a slope, `r_site[A,Intercept]`
  is $a_A$, and `sigma` is $\sigma_e$. `variables(fit)` lists them all.
- **$\sigma$ with AR(1) errors.** `brms` reports the innovation SD
  $\sigma_e$; `nlme` and `glmmTMB` report the SD of the total error,
  $\sigma_e/\sqrt{1-\phi^2}$. Convert before comparing.
- **Gaps in time.** `ar()` treats the observed times within a group as
  consecutive. Add rows for the missing times with `y = NA` and use
  `y | mi()` (section 4).
- **Compile time.** Every new `brm()` model compiles. Use `file =` to
  save fits and `update()` for new data.
- **Few groups.** With fewer than about five levels, the posterior for a
  random-effect SD follows its prior. Report the prior and check how
  much the answer moves under a wider or narrower one. Expect the
  posterior median of an SD to sit above the ML estimate when there are
  few groups: the posterior is right-skewed and averages over the
  other parameters.
- **Binomial syntax.** `brms` needs `s | trials(n)` for counts out of
  $n$; `cbind(s, n - s)` is an error there. `rstanarm` takes the
  `glmer()` form.
- **Factors.** Make grouping variables factors, and give nested units
  unique labels (or use `site/plot`), as in `lme4`.

**Learn more:** Bürkner (2017, *J. Stat. Software* 80(1)) and the
`brms` vignettes (`vignette(package = "brms")`); the `rstanarm`
vignettes, especially *Estimating Generalized (Non-)Linear Models with
Group-Specific Terms with rstanarm*; McElreath (2020), *Statistical
Rethinking*, 2nd ed.; Gelman et al. (2020), *Bayesian Workflow*
(arXiv:2011.01808).
